passage:
Teacher's note. In debate club today the class asked Keerthana, "Which side are you on?" It was said like a dare. Keerthana glanced at the floor, then said, "I agree with parts of both. I'm still learning." A few classmates rolled their eyes. Keerthana looked uneasy but did not pick a side. After class I said that "still learning" is an honest and respectable answer, and I gave Keerthana a short reading list with writers from several views. I also told the group that nobody has to join a team today. I'll ask next week what Keerthana found.
- Sahil, civics teacher

qa.q: What did Keerthana say when asked which side to join?
qa.a: Keerthana said, "I agree with parts of both. I'm still learning."

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling in that moment, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Keerthana felt pressured and uneasy, glancing at the floor, but held to the honest answer.

qa.q: What did Sahil do to help, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Sahil called "still learning" respectable and gave a reading list from several views, since reading widely is stronger than joining a team early.

qa.q: How might the classmates who asked see Keerthana's answer?
qa.a: Some may see it as dodging, as the eye-rolling suggests, though they may also just want company on their side.

grounding: Keerthana holds views that fit neither side and feels pressure to pick; the teacher affirms 'still learning' and offers wide reading.

passage:
I'm Jyoti, and in Class 11 I felt like the only person in school who didn't have a team.

Our class group argued about everything: fuel prices, new laws, whose leader was worse. I agreed with one side about some things, like public transport, and with the other side about others, like small businesses. When I said that at lunch, Minakshi rolled her eyes. "You can't have it both ways. Pick one."

I went home confused. Was I just weak? Everyone else seemed so sure.

My Dadu, who reads three newspapers every morning, laughed when I told him. "I'm seventy-two and still learning. Why should you be finished at sixteen?"

So I started reading the editorials from both sides on Sundays, and a book from the library about how policies actually get made. When Minakshi asked again, I said, "I'm still learning. I'll tell you when I know."

She didn't like it. But I felt steadier than I had in months.

qa.q: How many newspapers does Dadu read every morning?
qa.a: Dadu reads three newspapers every morning.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling after Minakshi said to pick one side?
qa.a: Jyoti felt confused and pressured, wondering whether not having a team meant being weak.

qa.q: What did Jyoti start doing that was wise, and why?
qa.a: Jyoti started reading editorials from both sides and a library book on how policies are made, because reading widely is stronger than joining a team early.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Jyoti says they are still learning?
qa.a: Minakshi seems frustrated and impatient, since she wants people to take a clear side.

grounding: It shows a teen whose views do not fit either side and who feels pressured to pick, choosing to say they are still learning and to read widely.

passage:
Civics teacher's note, Class 10, after the class debate

In the Friday debate, the class split into two loud camps. Yash stayed at his desk. When Ganga, who led one side, called out, "Yash, which side are you? You can't sit on the fence," the whole room turned to him.

He went red. "I agree with some of both," he said. Someone laughed. "Fence-sitter."

After class he stayed back and asked me, "Is it bad that I don't know? Everyone else has a side."

I told him it isn't bad. Knowing you're still learning is honest, and many adults would be wiser if they said it more. I gave him three articles from different viewpoints on the same issue and asked him to tell me next week what each one leaves out.

On Monday he came back with notes in the margins. In the next discussion, when Ganga asked again, he said calmly, "Still learning. But I've read both sides now." Ganga paused, then said, "Okay, tell me what you read."

qa.q: What did someone call Yash when he said he agreed with some of both?
What was Yash feeling when the whole room turned to him?
qa.a: Yash felt embarrassed and pressured, going red when asked to pick a side.

qa.q: How did the civics teacher help Yash?
qa.a: The teacher said it is fine to still be learning and gave him three articles from different viewpoints to compare.

qa.q: How might Ganga see Yash's answer on Monday?
qa.a: Ganga seems curious rather than dismissive now, asking him what he read, because he has clearly done the work.

grounding: It shows a teen whose views fit neither side and who is pressed to pick, saying he is still learning and reading widely instead.
